title: cache warmth is a setting, not something to poll for: main conversation gets 1h on a subscription, subagents get 5m unless subagentPromptCacheTtl says otherwise
what: Docs, prompt-caching page: every cache hit resets the TTL, so no message from a person is needed to keep one warm. Main conversation defaults to 1h on a subscription within plan usage and drops to 5m on usage credits; promptCacheTtl restores it. Subagents, forks, compaction and titles sit in the other bucket at 5m by default; subagentPromptCacheTtl, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL or a per-agent experimental cacheTtl raise it to 1h. A subagent never reads the parent cache; a fork does. Cache is scoped to machine and working directory and carries the startup git snapshot, so per-round sessions in one workspace can still hit the system prompt and project context.

title: Adapt works on its own tooling and rules only through the inbox; no instance ratifies its own request; tests are built at skill initialization; the manager's task file is the status surface

title: answered q3: When a round dies mid-way, should the next round clean up its worktrees and reopen the work item by itself, or should wreckage
what: Question (2026-09-16T00:28:11): When a round dies mid-way, should the next round clean up its worktrees and reopen the work item by itself, or should wreckage always wait for you to look at it? How many automatic retries before the item is parked for you? Answer (2026-09-16T00:33:49): Should perform a rollback of changes that occurred during the run - if this is easy to do, otherwise I think the manager itself should get involved in the process of establishing the current status of work done within the previously active folders/environments. Work should always be getting logged to the history.jsonl files and active areas should be noted as active so that in the event of some kind of crash the overarching state and where changes have been occurring should be discoverable. I think the manager with its greater reasoning capabilities will be best used in this particular case to resolve the crash and determine what needs to be rolled back. If we have an automated and easy rollback method that can all be done as code then that is preferrable to having an agent try and rectify the crashed state. It is better to just redo the round from a known state than it is to try and salvage one that was in progress.

title: answered q7: Which acts should wait for your approval: creating a new skill, deleting or changing a rule, merging into a skill you rely on,
what: Question (2026-09-16T00:28:11): Which acts should wait for your approval: creating a new skill, deleting or changing a rule, merging into a skill you rely on, or none of them? And do you want a notice when a round finishes or stalls, or is watching the manager's task file enough? Answer (2026-09-16T01:04:51): Adapt is a skill that is primarily for the user's external host agent and not for the user itself. To that end, the manager instance of adapt should not report back necessarily to the user but to the external host agent. The main division between the external host agent and the adapt agents is based around the interface and implementation split. The host agent should really only be concerned with its intent, the api surface that adapt provides through the skills it maintains, and how well that surface seems to fulfill the host agent's intent. Beyond this, the host agent should really not care, because anything below that level into the implementation is not relevant to its own work. It is just a user of the skills - if they work then they work. It does not care how they work. The manager is responsible for more of the grand internal designs and how they may affect the ease, expediency, and token usage costs for delivering fixes, and capabilities to the external user.

Answer (2026-09-16T01:13:03): The default is to keep separate all of these runtime developments. So new or modified or deleted rules, findings, tools etc. are all per host project and should remain that way. That is a core part of the adapt tool. title: answered q8: What is a work item, concretely? Is it a task in the manager's task window, or its own file that a task points at? What does it
what: Question (2026-09-16T01:54:51): What is a work item, concretely? Is it a task in the manager's task window, or its own file that a task points at? What does it carry beyond the acceptance criteria, and what states does it pass through from drafted to closed or parked? Answer (2026-09-16T14:12:49): work items. should be instance / machine facing objects that specialists can know and understand easily. Maybe a structured format like json to confer information - open to other suggestions. The request entries that come into the inbox are read by the manager. I think all requests are read before any action is taken. Notes are written as these are read. In the case that the request is a new or extension feature request, The manager should first consider if the request is something that can already be done by an existing skill that the external host may not be familiar with or have no knowledge of and can instead provide a follow up response to the external host with the api surface and some short documentation that addresses the initial request - then close out the request. This is one avenue. If it cannot point the external instance to an existing api surface, then that is where the manager considers engineering effort. It should have a great understanding of the api surface of all sibling skills and be able to consider internals of those skills by potentially drawing on graph information now provided by graphifyy. Skill information should be high level. Not sure, but maybe we should make this usable by the manager in the event that a specialist is not instantiated and does not already have a graph available to read. All work items (folders) should be tracked by the manager as tasks. Tasks (not sure if linking is presently implemented) should be linked to the work of other folders/subfolders in the case where a task is drilled down into. So for the manager its task is a single entry of work item, but that work item will be retrieved and read by a specialist that the manager invokes and that specialist will take that work item and as part of its protocol - "processify" the implementation into tasks of its own. Those sub tasks are recorded in the same rules-system ledger of the tasks.md that the specialist owns and should have its current task file linked against the entry of the work folder that exists. The manager's task entry will point to a separate folder, which will contain all running information about the current task. The structure around this entry will have automated fixtures that return data from the specialist and in some cases multiple specialists that work on the entry. There will exist a history.jsonl file that contains the running log of events pulled straight from the history files of the constituent specialists that are working on the item. There will be something of a spec file that the manager helps build which is a coarse grain process of what the specialists must do to build out the work item (if its new or an extension). In the case of a repair the manager could provide some high level guidance on how to probe and narrow down the code area for which the issue may be occurring (could use graphiffy information to provide this direction ). There should also be a group communication file channel that can post messages as a sequence of entries similar to the history file, where each instance can query the file for new entries that it has not yet seen and can retrieve them in the order they were written. Also commands to submit group messages. I am not sure what exact states the work item will contain. I think that is maybe less interesting. The work entry itself as a folder can be retired or parked into folders that help sort it out by its end state. Fulfilled vs Aborted vs Postponed, or some similar folder states. The idea behind the work item is to separate out information specific to the request/entry/current repair, extension, or new work from the home folder of either the manager or the specialists, this way the information domains are distinct. If information derived during the process of doing the work is useful to know by either the manager or the specialist it can be deposited into either home folder to help with future work, or promoted to a rule, through the candidate request process. Acceptance criteria as tests should be a major gate for completion. I think the manager can design the final test that should pass and append that test on to the test suite that the specialist will run after performing its work and thinking its work done. This might be a better job for another testing specialist agent that has a breadth of knowledge on how to properly construct tests and extra context on preventing the instance from making tests that are trivially easy to satisfy or that are gamed in some way. The original copy of the request should be in the folder work entry. I am sure other information can also be deposited into this folder too as we consider it more deeply.

title: answered q10: Should a round leave its own folder behind, holding the work item, the evidence, the verifier's result and the closing report?
what: Question (2026-09-16T01:54:53): Should a round leave its own folder behind, holding the work item, the evidence, the verifier's result and the closing report? Or should the round exist only as entries in the manager's history, stamped with a round id? Answer (2026-09-16T14:49:26): Yes we can create a folder for the manager specifically that holds rounds. Maybe a simple file for now that just contains references to work items through ids, or file references. This should be autogenerated. Mostly for us to use as diagnostic information so we can refine the whole skill and for the instances to help refine their own workflows within the skill. Rounds should try to be stateless in that the preceding work of a past round should not have a follow up in the next. The instances of a round should only concern themselves with the work of the round and nothing from previous rounds. If there are now work items then the manager could as part of its protocol go through the round files and use information there to determine future improvements or changes to the current system based on what it uncovers. I think that maybe these round items could be folders and could contain the old history of previous manager rounds, task files, and questions. Then when a new round starts all of the current files for the manager are wiped clean and the old ones are kept in the round folder. - I don't think we need any kinds of closing reports. Maybe a line for each task to say what was attempted and what was done (single word status for each), so that the history log does not need to be deciphered to determine that. Managers should contain tasks also of the agent spin up, research, design considerations, and other items too that will exist in their task logs.

title: define the round record: its id and what it leaves behind
result: user: rounds are stateless toward each other; each leaves an autogenerated folder in the manager's rounds folder with references to its work items and the manager's archived history, task and question files, and the next round starts with empty ones; round folders are diagnostic, and an idle round may mine them for improvements
